extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Restoration drama / literary scholars interested in Dryden and 17th-century theatre
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading and assessment of a Restoration-era play text (Dryden's The Assignation) including editorial footnotes and prologue/dedication commentary that bear on literary taste, originality, and theatrical reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Originality consists in the mode of treating a subject, more than in the subject itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As argued in the commentary: two authors may treat the same source material but originality is judged by how the subject is handled. Langbaine's criticism (that characters are imitated from Scarron) is countered by the claim that form and treatment, not mere subject-matter, determine originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dedicating plays (rhetorical strategy and propriety)
rubrics_metrics.description: The design of dedicating plays is as common and unjust, as that of desiring seconds in a duel. It engages friends in a senseless quarrel where they have much to venture, without any concernment of their own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dryden advises modesty and caution in dedications: do not obligate a patron to defend a work, avoid flattering that forces a friend into an awkward position, and treat the dedication as a means of securing posterity's record rather than immediate defence. Ancient models (Horace, Ovid) used praise of contemporaries to cement reputations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and tone of the prologue / audience expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Prologues, like bells to churches, toll you in With chiming verse, till the dull plays begin; ... You damn the poet, but the priest damns you: But priests can treat you at your own expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prologue frames the play and explicitly comments on what Restoration audiences expect and enjoy: exaggerated fops and buffoonery, stock fools (Mamamouchi), and spectacle. The text warns that audiences often applaud performances/novelties while condemning the poet, and that dramatic success often depends on giving the audience the fashionable kinds of characters and noisy show rather than subtlety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of blasphemy and atheism as poor tactic
rubrics_metrics.description: For blasphemy and atheism, if they were neither sin nor ill manners, are subjects so very common, and worn so threadbare, that people, who have sense, avoid them, for fear of being suspected to have none.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat controversial themes like blasphemy and atheism cautiously: they are overused and damage a writer's perceived judgment and reputation. Dryden suggests sensible writers avoid these topics because their repetition signals lack of wit rather than courage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candour, praise, and sociability among poets
rubrics_metrics.description: The poets of that age enjoyed much happiness in the conversation and friendship of one another... their discourse is neither too serious nor too light, but always pleasant, and, for the most part, instructive; the raillery, neither too sharp upon the present, nor too censorious on the absent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literary practice should value candour, balanced raillery, and mutual praise; social exchange (genial evenings) is both pleasurable and instructive. Dryden invokes classical models who praised contemporaries as a mark of social/artistic virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting theatrical failure: text vs. performance vs. reception
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the fault was in the play itself, or in the lameness of the action, or in the number of its enemies, who came resolved to damn it for the title, I will not now dispute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat a poor reception as conclusive proof of a bad text: failures may result from weak staging/action, hostile audiences/critics, or unlucky fortune. Evaluation of a play should distinguish textual merit from production and sociopolitical circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popularity and spectacle vs. critical taste
rubrics_metrics.description: The jargon of the songs, like similar nonsense of our own day, seems to have been well received on the stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Popular success (e.g., acceptance of nonsensical song-jargon or flamboyant spectacle) does not necessarily indicate high literary quality. Critics should recognize the difference between what pleases a crowd and what merits praise from refined taste; authors may be plagiarized or pander to fashion yet still gain an audience.
